index.note: Flow opens the room: what Amber Shockey & Co. makes and what these patterns are, then three chapters, one per collection, that are also the section titles; each opens to its motif and how it pairs, black linework carries a plain line, and the closing keeps its head so its marks don't land under red dragons.
abs: Amber Shockey & Co. is a startup, and every new collection has to sit next to the ones before it.

Each collection sets something structured against something organic, with a hero pattern, a secondary, and an accent. They run in several colorways, so the same set can go minimal or maximal depending on what it's paired with.

The blue florals collection.t: The blue florals collection layers pattern on pattern,
li: The peony | the biggest motif, and it looks like wallpaper when the pattern runs large.
On the plate | a peony border around a geometric center.
With black linework | blue florals go with it when the table needs some structure.

Black linework is the simplest.t: Black linework is the simplest of the three,
Black linework is the simplest.g: and it can be the setting under blue florals or red dragons
li: No florals | the only collection without them.
The halftone dot | the plainest motif, density made from dots.
The ground | flat and graphic, so either one keeps its color on top of it.

The red dragons statement plate.t: Burgundy dragons curl through floral filigree,
The red dragons statement plate.g: and the statement plate is for a buyer who only wants one piece
li: The dragons | they sit in a round mandala borrowed from Eastern textile work, in the most ornamental of the three collections.
Next to blue florals | the cobalt and the burgundy fight, so cream pieces from either collection go between the two.
